title: Karol G’s 200 Copas Tequila: Price, Where to Buy and the Story Behind the Bottle - ColombiaOne.com
content: Colombian reggaeton star Karol G surprised her fans with the launch of her own tequila brand: 200 Copas, inspired by her hit song of the same name. Over the past two days, the artist had kept her followers in suspense after sharing on her Instagram stories an image of a dark blue glass bottle with the caption: “What started with a song.” Many speculated it was a fragrance inspired by her track Tu perfume. However, Karol G officially confirmed that it was her entry into the spirits industry with 200 Copas by Casa Dragones. True to her reputation for surprising fans, the Colombian artist announced her new project through a video filmed in an agave field, where she spoke about the essence of 200 Copas. In the post, she shared: “Today, after almost three years of working on this, I can finally announce that 200 Copas, our tequila, is a reality.” The announcement sparked a wave of positive reactions on social media, with fans celebrating the launch and saying they can’t wait to toast and sing 200 Copas while enjoying the tequila. The product is an ultra-premium crystalline tequila, crafted from 100% Blue Weber agave. It is aged for more than 12 months in custom-made American oak barrels, resulting in a flavor profile with notes of honey, almond, cooked agave, oak, and citrus. Une publication partagée par 200 Copas by Casa Dragones (@200copasbycasadragones) The 200 Copas packaging was designed as a tribute to the song that inspired it: a bonfire under a midnight blue sky. The bottle features Karol G’s 200 Copas tattoo engraved on it, while the box conceals the full lyrics of the song as a special detail for buyers. The collaboration between the singer and Casa Dragones—an ultra-premium small-batch tequila brand from Mexico — is further sealed with the signatures of Karol G and Bertha Gonzalez Nieves, CEO and co-founder of Casa Dragones, underscoring the authenticity and artisanal character of the project. The first edition of 200 Copas is being sold in limited quantities on a first-come, first-served basis through Casa Dragones’ official website. Its retail price is $119.99 USD, approximately 396,000 Colombian pesos. See all the latest news from Colombia and the world at   ColombiaOne.com. title: How Small Business Owners Are Using AI to Help Propel Growth - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. When Marie Hunter and her colleagues hit on a new idea earlier this year for her fuel distribution firm, she used an artificial intelligence (AI) agent to crunch the numbers. She wanted to add solar panels to the tanks to help power their pumps and make other modifications. Rather than analyzing the cost of customizing a few fuel storage tanks for select customers, the agent delivered an ambitious blueprint for a new business. “It came back with a plan to upsell a new product line of tanks with additional services,” says Hunter, the owner and president of KRG Oil Company, a small family firm outside Atlanta. The agent “is my force multiplier,” says Hunter. She jokingly named the agent Billi Jean, her take on the name of one of her favorite songs. Hunter developed the agent with a colleague and originally used it to help manage emails. It also analyzes finances and prepares strategic growth plans in line with Hunter’s vision for the company. In the last two years, small business owners such as Hunter are increasingly using AI to help shape the fortunes of their enterprises, according to a report released this month by Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses, an education and support program that has helped thousands of enterprises grow and create jobs. Hunter and the other 10,000 Small Businesses alumni interviewed in this article have been independently exploring and integrating AI into their companies. In a survey of graduates of the program, 42% of respondents say they use AI for financial analysis and business planning, which is more than double the rate in 2024. And more than half of respondents say they use the innovation to develop or research new projects and products, according to the report, The AI Economy is a Small Business Economy. Small business owners are rapidly putting AI to work. More than 85% of survey respondents say they use AI in some form. Accounting for 43.5% of US economic output, small businesses are responsible for 61% of net new job creation, according to the US Small Business Administration’s Office of Advocacy. Small businesses are poised to play a significant role in the dissemination of AI. Asahi Pompey, global head of the Office of Corporate Engagement and chair of the Urban Investment Group, says the new Goldman Sachs Small Business AI Institute is designed to support small business owners as they navigate changes brought about by AI. The Institute will help guide entrepreneurs through AI adoption and integration, positioning them to push their businesses into this new frontier. “It is clear that AI is already changing how small business owners are making decisions, serving customers, and planning for growth,” she says. “The challenge is no longer whether small businesses will adopt AI. It is how they harness it fully and turn experimentation into lasting results.” Interviews with graduates of Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses show just how dynamic their AI applications are, and how strategically they have designed and deployed their own AI agents. The business owners are using AI to manage customer service at campgrounds, assist control rooms in petrochemical plants, and help design Spanish language lessons for online education. These businesses all share a common goal: using AI to get the most out of their businesses. Automation is nothing new for Bob McClure, the co-owner of McClure’s Pickles in Detroit. As the producer of more than 3 million jars of pickled cucumbers, onions, and peppers annually, the firm has long used industrial robots to label, pack, and stack its inventory. What is new is applying AI to the company’s critical functions, says McClure. Take food safety. Nothing is more important in his business, McClure says. The company constantly runs tests of its reporting system in the event of a food recall. In the past, employees manually entered information on the origins of the raw ingredients used to make pickles in a database, and it took 30 to 45 minutes to run a trace. After McClure integrated professional versions of large language models (LLMs) into the firm’s enterprise resource management program, the system could show the journey the ingredients took from their source to the jar in less than two minutes. It provides an online dashboard to show where the pickles were shipped, how much of the batch is left in the warehouse, and even its pH or acidity levels. McClure also used AI to create a maintenance application to automatically monitor production equipment, an accounting app to draft accounts payable for suppliers, and another app to review jar labels for accuracy. Integrating LLMs into business systems has its challenges There are challenges. Writing instructions for the LLMs takes finesse and sometimes a few “iterations” are needed to get it right. And sometimes there are bugs to work out. Because McClure, a former actor with no code training, can use natural language to engage the models, he says he does not need to license software or pay a technician. He can do it himself. Even better, he says he can apply the AI models to multiple tasks without paying more for their services. “I think AI is uniquely suited to small business entrepreneurship because you are so strapped for resources in terms of time, people, and money,” McClure says. “I now need to hire humans to manage my AI.” Naomi Stone, the owner and CEO of an environmental engineering consulting firm in Hermosa Beach, California, has gone a step further. She has made an AI application the cornerstone of a new venture, a company called Enso. Companies already pay to dispose of their surplus materials, and Stone says Enso is designed to turn that expense into a new revenue stream. The firm uses AI to match companies holding surplus materials and industrial byproducts with buyers who can put them to work. Some byproducts, like coal ash, have long been used to strengthen building materials. Other byproducts, from packaging to equipment to manufacturing scrap, simply need the right buyer, she says. For Stone, putting waste materials back to work advances the circular economy, a key tenet in sustainable finance. AI can facilitate matches between coal ash producers and buyers at a speed and scale Enso would have a hard time doing on its own. “It makes matches we haven’t even thought of,” says Stone. “And the best part is it can help our clients convert waste from a cost into a new revenue stream.” AI’s potential to illuminate unforeseen opportunities is a theme that comes up regularly among small business owners. Back in Roswell, Georgia, Marie Hunter says she has considered focusing more on her coaching business for entrepreneurs. So she gave her AI agent new instructions: to compile M&A data and prepare KRG Oil for an exit. “What does that look like, and what do I need to think about?” Hunter says. She adds that she’s ready to aspire to get her company to “the multiple it deserves.” Survey data is based on responses from 2,473 Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses alumni who participated in the 2026 Alumni Survey, conducted by Babson College from August 10–24, 2026. title: Why Luxury Goods Companies’ Revenues Are Forecast to Climb - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The outlook for luxury brands is improving after several years of lackluster performance, according to Goldman Sachs Research. A basket of large, publicly traded luxury-goods makers is forecast to increase revenue by 7% in 2027, Erwan Rambourg, head of Europe Luxury and Lifestyle in Goldman Sachs Research, writes in a report. This is an improvement from an expected 6% growth rate in 2026, when the sector came out of several years of weaker performance. “We view this as a solid recovery for an industry that has faced a prolonged period of sluggish performance,” Rambourg writes. The market capitalization for luxury-goods stocks increased in 2022, after the stock market swoon caused by the Covid pandemic. Luxury stocks benefited from “exuberant spending,” Rambourg notes, but this was followed by a period of aggressive price increases and a slower pace of innovation from the sector. Luxury-goods makers’ share prices have fallen over the past three or four years, but so have earnings estimates, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The result is that valuations do not look particularly attractive, and they also don’t appear stretched. “But we think valuation alone is rarely a catalyst for investors to buy or sell shares in the sector,” Rambourg writes. “Instead, it is more a function of sales momentum, which we see picking up soon.” The industry has faced multiple challenges. China’s ongoing property slump, US tariffs in 2025, jittery equity markets, upcoming midterm elections and higher rates, as well as the ongoing Middle East conflict and other geopolitical tensions have weighed on spending decisions. “There have been many reasons for consumers to cancel or delay purchases of discretionary products,” Rambourg writes. Still, these broader factors probably haven’t been the main constraint, he says, attributing the weak performance in recent years mostly to “a degree of strategic inertia” among luxury brands. Price hikes after the Covid pandemic, which were perceived as excessive by some observers, likely played a larger role in the slowdown in growth for luxury goods. More affordable luxury brands benefited as traditional high-end names hiked prices—estimated at around 60% between mid-2019 and mid-2026—opening space in the market that they could fill, according to Goldman Sachs Research. “As a direct impact of elevated price points and a value proposition that became less compelling across many brands, it appears that many target consumers decided to pass on purchasing luxury goods,” Rambourg writes. Alongside the aggressive price increases, limited innovation by the industry in the post-Covid period led to diminished consumer interest, and store traffic tailed off. That said, a number of luxury companies have new CEOs and creative directors who started presenting their collections last year. “We believe that it likely takes three to four collections for consumers to recognize—and possibly buy into—the change,” Rambourg writes. For many years there has been “a surprising disconnect between wealth in the US (high) and luxury demand among American consumers (low),” Rambourg points out. The market was likely restrained by a “guilt factor” or by “outlet culture,” he says. However, behaviors have begun to change since the Covid pandemic. “The appetite of American consumers for luxury goods has picked up strongly,” he writes. Luxury brands have taken notice, and store openings are multiplying. “While it may sound counterintuitive, we still think the US is an emerging market for luxury goods,” he adds. Elsewhere in the world, South Korean demand growth may be somewhat fragile because it is linked to wealth in the country’s tech-heavy and volatile equity market. The importance of Hong Kong for luxury brands has diminished over time, but the market is showing signs of recovery, with both local consumers and visitors from mainland China supporting sales growth, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The luxury goods companies Goldman Sachs Research covers have recorded average top-line growth of 6% annually over the past 25 years. “While growth has been pedestrian of late,” sales levels exceed what a 6% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) would have implied since just before the Covid pandemic in 2019, Rambourg points out. “In other words, the bear argument that the sector may have gone ex-growth for an extended period is not one we agree with,” he writes. To help understand where the sector and individual luxury goods makers may be headed, the report includes a benchmarking framework. This provides a way to think about long-term growth drivers, broken down as seven Cs. One of the Cs is clout, and Rambourg posits that “big is beautiful” in the luxury sector. He notes that bigger brands not only tend to secure better locations, but they also benefit from lower rent as a percentage of sales. Another is categories, with some consumer verticals, such as jewelry, having better growth potential than others, such as beauty products. Other considerations in the framework include: consumer caliber, referencing the relative resilience of high-net-worth consumers, which can likewise make high-end brands more resilient; and creativity, which may be difficult for equity analysts to quantify but does come into play in assessing prospects for luxury companies. Rounding out the list are consistency, which gets to the clarity of brand positioning; codes and icons, which are not necessarily loud logos but can be a discreet symbol, pattern, or logo only identifiable by people who know the products well; and finally, corporate considerations, as many luxury-goods companies are partly owned and run by family members. title: Birdie G’s Finds Its Next Chapter at Fairmont Century Plaza - Locale Magazine
content:
Birdie G’s, the beloved concept from James Beard-nominated Chef Jeremy Fox, officially opens at Fairmont Century Plaza on Oct. 26, ushering in a dynamic new culinary chapter at the property. Reimagined as an expansive American brasserie serving breakfast, lunch and dinner, the new Birdie G’s brings its signature creativity and spirit to Century City. Named for Fox’s daughter Birdie and his grandmother Gladys, Birdie G’s is known for its nostalgic yet inventive approach to American comfort cuisine rooted in family tradition, regional flavors and meticulous craftsmanship. Fox is a Food & Wine Best New Chef and a widely respected voice in California’s produce-driven cooking movement, and he originally opened the restaurant in 2019 at Bergamot Station. Born in Cleveland and raised across the Midwest and Deep South before settling in California, he draws on his personal journey, regional foodways and childhood memories of family meals and classic chain restaurants to craft a thoughtful and fun dining experience. At Fairmont Century Plaza, Birdie G’s evolves into an inviting neighborhood institution that honors the timeless spirit of classic Midwest supper clubs, where comfort, effortless polish and welcoming ease converge. Designed in partnership with EDG Design, the airy, light-filled space combines 1970s revival and midcentury sophistication with warmth and lived-in comfort. Comfy banquettes pair with warm rust and brown tones, custom leather touches and clean lines. The custom green plaid barstools are a playful nod to the exact interior of Fox’s original 1969 VW Beetle. The result is a fun, relaxed atmosphere that blends family traditions with Midwest Nice and Southern Hospitality. “In a lot of ways, this is more Birdie G’s than the original Birdie G’s,” Fox says. “The look and feel we always imagined never quite came together the first time, and here it finally has. You walk out of this sleek, modern lobby and step back in time into your grandparents’ rumpus room, with knick-knacks on the walls and all the little details that tell the story of where this food comes from. It’s the kind of place you have to experience in person, and I can’t wait to welcome everyone in to see it for themselves.” The menu features timeless American dishes transformed by Fox’s innovative techniques, handcrafted production and commitment to local, sustainable ingredients from regional farmers, ranchers and artisans. Breakfast features comforting morning classics with subtle deli and diner undertones. The Smoked Fish Platter comes with a bagel, cucumber, cherry tomato, pickled onion, roe, capers, crème fraîche, chives and dill. The Cornbread Waffle arrives with sweet pepper jam and popcorn butter, and the Brûléed French Toast is topped with spiced apple, Spanish peanuts and smoked cinnamon chantilly. For something heartier, Steak & Eggs pairs a koji-marinated hanger steak with two eggs any style, breakfast potatoes and three peppercorn sauce. Lunch can be friendly and casual or an elevated executive experience for the Century City business crowd. Crisp seasonal salads include The Century Plaza Wedge with little gems, smoked bacon, deviled egg mousse, cherry tomato, red onion, scallion and Bay Blue cheese. There’s also a Chopped Antipasto Salad that can be topped with salmon, hanger steak or chicken breast. Signature entrees include the Birdie Burger & Fries with onion jam, shaved onion, Cooper sharp cheddar and AL’s steak sauce, along with a Croque Madame and the Corned Beef Tongue Reuben. Both lunch and dinner feature The Pickle Chick, a gluten-free schnitzel with cucumber, cornichon, whipped feta, dill pickle sauce, horseradish and dill pollen. Both menus also offer Prime Steak Frites made with prime Flannery beef grilled with a Montreal rub and served with fries and aioli. Cuts include an 8-ounce hanger, a 12-ounce New York strip and a 28-ounce bone-in Jorge Ribeye dry-aged for 28 days. Each comes with your choice of sauce, including AL’ Steak Sauce, Horsey Cream, Pot Roast Butter and Three Peppercorn. The evening menu highlights generous portions and elegant cuts of steaks and chops, poultry and seafood. The Lamb a la Saless features a fat-capped lamb saddle marinated in fenugreek, black lime and beet molasses, served with crispy dill rice, dates and saffron yogurt. Mt. Lassen Trout comes with potato, smoked trout roe sauce and chive, and Chicken & Vegetables From the Rotisserie is served with root stoemp, cabbage, schmaltz, gribenes and beurre poulet. Inventive vegetable dishes include Sprouting Broccoli with miso bagna cauda and hippy seed mix. The Fioretto Cauliflower Kugel is a casserole of duck egg noodles baked with four-cheese mornay, garlic confit and bread crumbs. Fan favorites make an appearance too, like Fresh Cucumbers pickled to order in dill pickle sauce and Matzo Ball Soup served with one golden spoon. To start, there’s Bub & Grandma’s Bread or Five-Onion Dip & Potato Chips, which can be topped with N25 caviar. The menu pays homage to Fox’s culinary journey with an extra touch of hospitality: here, a Birdie’s dozen means 14. The restaurant’s iconic desserts remain an essential part of the menu. The World-Famous Rose Petal Pie is a terrazzo of raspberry, hibiscus and strawberry gelées in rosewater cream with a buttered pretzel crust. It’s joined by the nostalgic Malted Chocolate Layer Cake and the Sticky Date Bundt Cake with salted caramel sauce, because nobody has ever complained about too much caramel. The Creamsicle Rice Pudding comes with market citrus, coconut milk, preserved lemon and orange blossom, and at dinner, look for the Sugar Cream Tart, which the menu describes as crème brûlée in a pie crust. Since the restaurant is named for Fox’s daughter, young diners are treated with equal reverence. The dedicated kids menu offers thoughtfully made Potato-Crusted Chicken Fingers, pasta, Matzo Pizza Margherita and the playful Healthy Yucky Green Salad. The bar program leans into farmers market produce and a variety of housemade infused spirits, syrups and tinctures. The cocktail menu serves nostalgic classics alongside modern creations. Morning sips include a Bloody Mary made with the restaurant’s signature mix and Hibiscus Heat with lime, agave, citrus, tequila blanco and habanero. There’s also Spritzing in Sunny Century City with Carpano Bianco, Mommenpop blood orange and sparkling wine. The wine list ranges from global classic vintages to unique selections from winemakers dedicated to soil health. Birdie G’s is open daily, with coffee starting at 6 a.m. Breakfast and lunch are served from 6:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., and dinner runs from 5:30 to 9 p.m. Reservations are available on OpenTable. For private events, email events@birdiegsla.com. Celebrating its 60th anniversary in 2026, Fairmont Century Plaza stands as a reimagined icon following a $2.5 billion renovation. The property features 400 expansive guest rooms with private terraces, 63 luxury residences and the 14,000-square-foot Fairmont Spa Century Plaza. It also offers 24,000 square feet of private event space, including one of the largest ballrooms in Los Angeles. The hotel was originally built in 1966 on the site of a former 20th Century Fox Studios backlot. It has hosted legendary moments, from the Beatles winning big at the 10th Annual Grammy Awards to the Presidential State Dinner hosted by President Nixon to honor the Apollo 11 astronauts. title: 310-HP V6, AWD, Torque Vectoring - Buick's Final Sports Sedan Costs Half As Much As A New Golf R - CarBuzz
content: We added a section with one more powerful luxury sedan that's worth around $20k on the used market. If there's one thing that we gearheads can agree on, it's that new car prices are ridiculous. In fact, the average price for a new car in the US has hit $50,000. That's almost exactly the price of a new  Volkswagen Golf R, and while it may be fast, safe, and comfortable, what if your money were best spent on something used? Something a bit more practical with similar performance, perhaps? Enter: the Buick Regal GS. This American sports sedan was more than a rebadged European family car, offering performance and space without the high price tag. You can now easily find this car for less than half the price of a used Golf R – something we still can't quite understand. Here's why... Buick knew that time was running out for its sedans in the 2010s. The automaker's SUV sales were surging, and while the fifth-gen Regal sedan was a great car, its looks were becoming outdated and customers started looking elsewhere. That's why in 2017, the sixth-generation Regal debuted with a much more handsome exterior and interior. The writing was on the wall for this car, which is why Buick decided to go out with a bang. The GS trim was introduced as the halo version, featuring a larger 3.6L V6 engine and sportier cosmetics. While we think of ultra-exclusive Italian supercars as collectibles, the Regal GS's low production number of around 1,300 means it's exclusive and represents perhaps the last true performance-oriented Buick like this. For the company that gave us the GNX and Skylark GS, it's safe to say that collectors love the last-of-the-line model.But nostalgia alone doesn't justify a purchase – so what does the GS actually deliver behind the wheel? The GS badge meant the Regal was ready to be driven hard. Its 3.6L V6 engine has strong links to the Chevrolet Colorado and GMC Canyon of the same vintage, but here it makes 310 horsepower and 282 lb-ft through a clever all-wheel-drive system. That AWD system isn't old-fashioned, either, as it has torque vectoring capabilities that mean it can send up to 100% of the engine's power to an individual rear wheel through two computer-controlled clutches. This AWD system is also used in the TourX wagon, but in the GS driving mode, it will send more of its power to the rear wheels. This driving mode also firms up the adaptive suspension, quickens throttle response, makes the steering heavier, and lets the nine-speed automatic hold onto gears longer. It's exactly what you want in a sports sedan – the ability to be comfortable in most situations and then turn into a sports car when asked. Beyond the engine and AWD system, there's a lot to love. The transmission is smooth, it can reach 60 miles per hour in under six seconds, and reaches a top speed of 167 miles per hour. The GS' Brembo brakes are also solid. Without turbochargers, the V6 produces linear power that you'll want to unleash. It makes peak torque at 5,200 rpm and peak power at 6,800 rpm, meaning it has that old-school rev-happy character. So, it's half the price of a new Golf R – is it half the amount of fun? Definitely not. The V6 in the GS makes only 18 hp and 13 lb-ft of torque less than Volkswagen's 2.0L turbo-four, and while it may be a second slower to 60 miles per hour, it offers much of the same on-paper performance. Of course, the Golf R's 4Motion all-wheel-drive system is much more modern and advanced, leading to super-grippy all-weather performance, but the Buick isn't far behind. The Regal's performance means it's easily faster than the Golf GTI, and while the modern hot hatches may be more agile, the Buick's slightly longer wheelbase may make it more stable at speed. Volkswagen offers the Golf R with standard adaptive suspension, meaning just like the Regal, it's a superb daily driver but turns into a monster when asked. The best thing about both the Regal GS and the Golf R is how they combine performance and everyday usability. This stretches to the design, as the GS badges on the Buick are subdued and, unless you were looking, you wouldn't be able to tell it's the flagship. The Golf looks a bit racier with its spoiler and vents, especially in a bright color that complements its stance. We love the design of both, but those wanting a sleeper will prefer the GS. Even with the younger Golf in comparison, the Buick Regal GS isn't as sparse as you may think. There's ventilated seating, keyless start, and most impressively, massage controls for both front seats. Of course, the Golf has the larger infotainment display, as that's where the industry is heading, but the GS has smartphone connectivity so you're not stuck with an outdated system. The only thing that we can see the Golf having over the Regal is rear heated seats and a better sound system. It's worth mentioning size, too, as the Buick wins easily here. The Golf manages just under 20 cubic feet of space in the cargo bay, while the GS can manage 31.5 cubes. It also has more rear legroom at 36.9 inches compared to 35 inches, and its hatchback design makes it highly practical. With only 1,300 units made, the Buick Regal GS isn't super common on the marketplace, so when one pops up, we'd certainly be reaching out quickly. You won't have to worry about high-mileage examples, either, as the LGX family of 3.6L V6 engines is said to be reliable when properly maintained. It's an improvement over previous GM blocks like this. Very high-mileage examples may benefit from a cleanup around the intake valves, which can clog with carbon buildup. Some owners also recommend getting the timing chain checked out, so a recent service stamp for this is ideal. Given its status as a sports sedan, make sure you're getting a well-cared-for example with service history. At the time of writing, we can see listings range from $20–$25k for cars with around 60,000 miles. You can dip under $20k if you go for listings with around 100,000 miles, and we wouldn't be worried about reliability with its decent record. Even if you find an unreliable example, you'll still be way under the Golf R's price with some repairs and servicing. Can you feel the 18 hp difference between these two cars by the seat of your pants? Probably not. The Regal GS is a more practical sleeper sedan that has just as many creature comforts as the Golf, without the intrusive new-car chimes and alerts. And for half the price, you can't go wrong. On the topic of affordable, luxurious, powerful sedans, we can't help but bring up the 2017–2020 Lincoln MKZ. It's technically built on the same boring platform as the Ford Fusion, but the MKZ's top trim level, the Reserve, was powered by the same engine found under the Ford Bronco Raptor's hood today. Drivers can enjoy a 3.0-liter twin-turbo V6 that makes 350 horsepower when paired with a front-wheel-drive drivetrain, or 400 horsepower with all-wheel drive. Flooring it from a stop sign results in a 4.8-second 0-60 mph sprint on its way to a 150 mph limited top speed. The best part of it all is that buyers can find a 2020 MKZ Reserve for around $20,000 today in average condition. title: Ali G’s crude comeback is one long, strained stunt - AOL.com
content: The only true surprise of the new Ali G film, which marks the directing debut of Sacha Baron Cohen, is that it is not entirely terrible. A couple of decades since Baron Cohen’s career-launching rude boy was last at large, he has contrived a comeback that delivers only scattered laughs and stray bursts of inspiration; the whole thing has the feel of a strained stunt. Reviving the mockumentary format where it all began, Ali G: Who Iz I? starts out pretending that the Staines-born cultural appropriator, who acts as though he is black despite being ethnically indeterminate, was cancelled around 2004. (In fact, the character was sensibly retired, after the feeble first spin-off film, Ali G Indahouse (2002) – a conventionally scripted lowbrow comedy – proved that he’d run out of road.) And so off Ali jets to Los Angeles, where he has the mistaken idea that HBO is keen to resurrect his series. It’s not a terrible idea to use Ali now as a confused exemplum of cancel culture. Especially since, right on cue, there have been calls for the new film to be boycotted, for the same reason that people have always found him offensive: namely, that Baron Cohen treads a fine line between satirising racial stereotypes and milking them. The new film, in which we see Ali allegedly punking a bunch of nobodies with stupid and/or revolting routines, is strangely desperate for us to know that a vast majority of the people he encounters are not “in on it”. But in on what, exactly? We presume that release forms were signed by everyone who appears on camera – and who knows what they were told. No single sit-down interview here (in the style now appropriated by Philomena Cunk) lasts longer than about 30 seconds. To switch things up, Baron Cohen introduces two new characters under prosthetics – a deranged Leftist professor and an ex-Mossad agent – who play like party tricks from the fag end of Mike Myers’s repertoire. Itching to unleash the crass gross-out comedy that Baron Cohen has been unable to resist since the first Borat, the film treats us to a baffling scenario in which two of his own characters are shown having sex, so that one can extract DNA from the other for an ancestry test. Ali’s hope of having actual black paternity – he gets it into his head that the 38-year-old rapper A$AP Rocky might be his father – is a more fruitfully absurd avenue, but we only get an end-credits cameo, with Rihanna (Rocky’s other half) providing the side-eye. It may only be the first race of a new season but it already feels like there is so much riding on the men’s Audi FIS World Cup Giant Slalom in Sölden on Sunday. Will newly crowned Olympic and World Cup champion Lucas Pinheiro Braathen (BRA/Atomic) continue his golden form and kickstart a tilt at this season’s Overall title? Might the equally in-form Loic Meillard (SUI/Rossignol) finally conquer the infamous Rettenbach Glacier and lay down a marker of his own? Which of the quartet of impressive Norwegians will emerge strongest? Can a Marco Schwarz (AUT/Atomic) free of Slalom considerations become Austria’s first winner of the home opener in 12 years? Is everyone mad to even countenance anything but another GS masterclass from Marco Odermatt (SUI/Stöckli)? All these questions, and more, will be answered when the action gets underway with the first run at 10:00 CET. For four seasons, 2022-2025, no one could get near Odermatt on GS skis. The Swiss megastar not only claimed a quartet of Crystal Globes, he did it in truly dominant style. The zenith came in 2023/24 when only a second run DNF in the World Cup Finals in Saalbach prevented Odi from completing an extraordinary season sweep. Two wins in the first three races last season suggested more of the same. But no one had told Pinheiro Braathen. From late December through to the final race in Lillehammer, the Brazilian went on a tear. A run of finishes that read 2nd-2nd-2nd-1st-1st propelled him up the GS standings and, thanks to that final-day victory when everything was on the line, past a bemused Odermatt. A first ever World Cup Globe for Brazil was accompanied by a first ever Olympic gold medal, with Pinheiro Braathen once again relegating the great Odermatt to second place. The challenge has well and truly been laid down. The sense of an epic rivalry only increased recently when Pinheiro Braathen made it clear he will add the Super G to his schedule in an attempt to also snatch Odi’s Overall crown. There is nowhere better than Sölden to kick it all off. While Odermatt is a master of the Rettenbach’s particular challenges and will chase a fourth win to tie Ted Ligety (USA) as the resort’s most successful male skier, Pinheiro Braathen has tasted success here too, winning in 2020. Not that the rest of a high quality field have any intention of letting the duo take over. GS world champion in 2019, GS Globe winner in 2020 and second in the standings in three of the past five seasons, Kristoffersen has all the attributes to muscle into the reckoning once more. “Until you beat (Ingemar) Stenmark on World Cup wins, I think there is always a goal to be had,” the 32-year-old said with a smile. “Of course, not every day is easy, but in the end the motivation is still there.” Part of a Norwegian clean sweep in Sölden two seasons ago and with another podium place in 2022, it would seem Kristoffersen knows how to get the most out of the early season stop. Even if the man himself is not entirely convinced. “The long step pitch is something special, and I’m not the best at stivoting, and I haven’t really cracked the code properly yet on how to do it turn after turn in Sölden. But we still keep on trying as best as we can,” he said, before adding, “Of course, there are hills which fit my style of skiing better.” There certainly are. Now happily on Head skis, Kristoffersen has won four World Cup GS races in Kranjska Gora and two in Alta Badia. Both are once more on the roster. Meillard is another with his eyes quietly on all sorts of prizes. The Swiss man has been electric over the past 18 months. Reigning Olympic and world Slalom champion, Meillard came mighty close to snatching last season’s GS World Cup Globe at the death. Add on the power of the nappy factor, and the 29-year-old is clearly one to watch. Meillard has finished in the top three in the GS Globe race in each of the past three seasons. A stat he almost matched in the Overall standings, with only a fourth-place finish last season dropping him off that podium. While Odermatt’s superb form in both the Downhill and Super G, alongside the GS, give him a clear advantage in the hunt for the Big Globe, his compatriot does have a chance to challenge him there too. “Tough to follow all three disciplines, be home, train, rest correctly, so, the focus at the beginning will be on Slalom and GS and then we will see as the season goes,” Meillard revealed in Sölden. “Definitely keeping it (the Super G) in my training (schedule) it definitely helps with GS to have that speed, and to be a bit more patient.” In somewhat of a contrast, it will be fascinating to see how Schwarz goes in Sölden, now that he has reduced his packed schedule from four disciplines to three. The 2021 Alpine combined world champion has dropped the Slalom, after three wins and 14 podium places in 105 World Cup starts. Sölden is not a bad place for his new adventure to start. Last year Schwarz became the first home hope to end on the podium in four years, and with a win following in Alta Badia, the Austrian clearly has the skills and confidence to challenge again. Fellow local, Stefan Brennsteiner (AUT/Fischer) is also in fine form. In fact, the 35-year-old has never been better. A win and six further top-five finishes propelled him to fourth in the GS standings last time out, his best ever finish in 11 seasons on tour. At the other end of the age scale, Alexander Steen Olsen’s (NOR/Rossignol) return to the starting line-up is a very welcome sight. The last time the 25-year-old competed in Sölden he won. A knee injury then kept the youngster out for the entirety of last season but he is now fit and firing once more. The battle for supremacy within the Attacking Vikings will be almost as fascinating as their efforts to top the rest of the field. Atle Lie McGrath (NOR/Head) finished off a wild season last time out with a brilliant Slalom Globe. The 26-year-old is yet to win a GS World Cup race, but he does have five podiums to his name, two of them coming in Sölden in the past two seasons. Timon Haugan (NOR/Van Deer) cannot yet match that GS consistency but he did finish last season with four top-five finishes in his final six races. Big names doing great things everywhere you look. Do not miss the start of the GS season, 10:00 CET Sunday.

title: GS Caltex Wins Seventh Women's Volleyball Cup - 조선일보
content: Hur Sae-hong's cultural visit refocused team for record title victory [Sports Chosun Kim Young-rok Reporter] Seventh overall cup tournament victory. GS Caltex continues its winning momentum this year, following last year's dramatic championship final victory. GS Caltex claimed the title by defeating Korea Expressway Corporation with a set score of 3-2 in the women's final of the 2026 Yeosu·NH Nonghyup Cup Professional Volleyball Tournament held at Jinnam Gymnasium in Yeosu, South Jeolla Province, on October 18. This marked the club's seventh cup tournament victory in its history, achieved after a three-year gap, and set a new record for the most titles in the women's division. Behind this victory lay a special story. On October 13, after completing the first preliminary round match, the team visited GS Caltex Yeulmaru and Art Island Jangdo, representative cultural and artistic spaces in Yeosu, as part of a schedule arranged by club owner Hur Sae-hong. The visit aimed to refresh the team's atmosphere and provide relaxation after their first group-stage match. GS Caltex Yeulmaru, whose name combines the meanings of "cultural waves" and "traditional wooden floors," is a complex cultural and artistic space established and operated by GS Caltex in Yeosu as part of its social contribution initiatives. It offers high-quality performances and exhibitions to locals and visitors, featuring a grand theater, small theater, and exhibition halls designed by world-renowned architect Dominique Perrault. Alongside Art Island Jangdo, it has become a representative cultural and artistic space in Yeosu. The team toured major facilities, including the grand theater and rehearsal hall at GS Caltex Yeulmaru, and took commemorative photos on the outdoor terrace. They then moved to Art Island Jangdo, timed to coincide with the opening of the sea path. The team toured the island's exhibition hall, enjoyed a pianist's performance at a café on Jangdo, and used the time to relieve tension and communicate with teammates. This visit, arranged by club owner Hur Sae-hong to encourage the team, became a meaningful opportunity to refocus their minds ahead of the final. GS Caltex, energized by the visit to GS Caltex Yeulmaru, immediately turned the situation around. The team went on a three-game winning streak starting from the match following the visit and lifted the seventh cup tournament trophy by defeating Korea Expressway Corporation in the final. After the victory, club owner Hur Sae-hong sent a congratulatory message to the team: "A valuable victory, we are proud of you." He praised the team's performance, teamwork, and relentless focus until the end, which led to the seventh cup tournament title. He also expressed gratitude to GS Caltex Yeosu Plant employees who supported the team in Yeosu and encouraged the team to achieve good results in the 2026-2027 regular season. title: Pope Leo XIV: "The commitment to marriage and the family is more urgent than ever" – VIDEO - Rome Reports
content: Home - Pope - Pope Leo XIV: "The commitment to marriage and the family is more urgent than ever" – VIDEO Following his surgical operation, Pope Leo XIV presided over the general audience in St. Peter's Square, where he continued his commentary on the document Gaudium et Spes. On this occasion, he focused on conjugal love and the value of the family. Dear brothers and sisters, good morning and welcome! The first think I would like to say is thank you!. Thank you for the support of your prayers. Thanks be to God for His generosity. Let us all renew our trust in God’s goodness and mercy. The pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes(GS) of the Second Vatican Council, having illustrated in the first part the dignity of the person and his or her vocation in the world, goes on to consider, in the second part, “in the light of the Gospel and of human experience”, some of the most pressing contemporary issues (cf. GS, 46). It focuses primarily on marriage and the family, in the conviction that “the well-being of the individual and of human and Christian society is intimately linked with the healthy condition of that community produced by marriage and family” (GS, 47). To this end, it does not merely reaffirm their values and aims, but proposes a renewed conception of marriage as an “intimate partnership of married life and love” (GS, 48). By incorporating the legal dimension of marriage as a contract, the foundation of this union is recognized in the “conjugal covenant”, understood as the “human act whereby spouses mutually bestow and accept each another” (ibid.). The mutual self-giving of man and woman, such that ‘they are no longer two but one flesh’ (Mt 19:6), underlies the requirement for “total fidelity” and the “unbreakable oneness” of the spouses, finding vivid expression in the procreation and upbringing of children (cf. GS, 48). As a reflection of the Divine Trinity, conjugal and parental love, through the Sacrament of Marriage, is “governed and enriched by Christ’s redeeming power”, so that spouses may love one another “just as He loved the Church and handed Himself over on her behalf” (ibid.). Having shed light on the reality of marriage in the light of Christ’s love, which is the truth of both human and divine love, Gaudium et Spes turns its attention to conjugal love and marital fruitfulness. Not limited to erotic attraction, which it nonetheless encompasses, conjugal love involves the entire will of the spouses, enlivening the affections of their hearts and expressing itself through sentiments and gestures of tenderness (cf. GS, 49). Embracing the good of the whole person of both man and woman, who are equal in dignity, this love pervades the entire life of the spouses, finding expression in acts proper exclusively to marriage (cf. ibid.). Whilst signifying integral love from person to person, the unique intimacy between the spouses fosters their mutual self-giving and enriches their shared joy (cf. ibid.). Furthermore, the fruitfulness of conjugal love is expressed in the procreation of children, “the supreme gift of marriage” (GS, 50). By transmitting and educating human life, which must never be rejected, spouses become “cooperators with the love of God the Creator, and are, so to speak, the interpreters of that love” (ibid.). Called to this human and Christian responsibility, they are bound to allow themselves to be guided by a sound judgement regarding their own good and that of their children, whether already born or yet to be born. Such a judgement, which, in the final analysis, the spouses themselves must form before God, requires that their conscience conform to divine law, as interpreted by the Magisterium of the Church in the light of the Gospel (cf. ibid.). The emphasis on loving communion and procreative fruitfulness within marriage leads the Council to rule out the possibility of there being “a true contradiction … between the divine laws pertaining to the transmission of life, and those pertaining to authentic conjugal love” (GS, 51) and to affirm, instead, that “when there is question of harmonizing conjugal love with the responsible transmission of life”, one must “preserve the full sense of mutual self-giving and human procreation in the context of true love” (ibid.). From this it follows both that “from the moment of its conception life must be guarded with the greatest care”, renouncing “abortion and infanticide”; and that “the acts themselves which are proper to conjugal love and which are exercised in accord with genuine human dignity must be honoured with great reverence” (ibid.). The teaching of Gaudium et Spes on the conjugal and family community thus goes on to highlight the social function of the family, defined as “a school of deeper humanity” and “the foundation of society” (GS, 52), calling upon all those with social responsibilities, especially in the political and cultural spheres, to fulfil their duty to “work efficiently for the welfare of marriage and the family” (ibid.). Dear friends, this task is more urgent than ever before. The Church is well aware of this, as shown by the pastoral concern of the Popes who have succeeded one another since the last Council, right up to the two Synodal Assemblies convened by Pope Francis, which were addressed again in recent days by the Heads of the Eastern Catholic Churches and the Presidents of the Episcopal Conferences. May the Holy Family of Nazareth enlighten us on our journey and protect families throughout the world. I extend a warm welcome to all the English-speaking pilgrims and visitors taking part in today’s Audience. Upon all of you and your families, I invoke the joy and peace of our Lord Jesus Christ.  God bless you all! Dear brothers and sisters, in our ongoing catechesis on Gaudium et Spes, today we consider the dignity of marriage and the family in the context of contemporary challenges.  The Council Fathers recognized that the well-being of all in society is closely linked to the health of marriage and the family, and sought to present a renewed vision of conjugal love as an intimate partnership which reflects the life of the Trinity and is rooted in and enriched by the redemptive power of Christ.  Let us, therefore, pray for God’s blessing and protection upon all families.

title: Pope Leo dives in to what Vatican II says on family - Aleteia EN
content: It's more urgent than ever to "work efficiently for the welfare of marriage and the family," the Pope says. And "the Church is well aware of this." Pope Leo continued with his reflections on Vatican II, taking up the themes from Gaudium et Spes on the family during a rather wet general audience held this October 21 in St. Peter's Square. Here below is a translation of his brief reflection. He began by thanking the faithful for their prayers, in light of his recent surgery and cancer diagnosis: Catechesis. The Documents of the Second Vatican Council. IV. Constitution Gaudium et Spes.  6. Commitment to the family in today’s society (GS, 47–52) Dear brothers and sisters, good morning and welcome! The first thing I would like to say is thank you!. Thank you for the support of your prayers. Thanks be to God for His generosity. Let us all renew our trust in God’s goodness and mercy. The pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes (GS) of the Second Vatican Council, having illustrated in the first part the dignity of the person and his or her vocation in the world, goes on to consider, in the second part, “in the light of the Gospel and of human experience”, some of the most pressing contemporary issues (cf. GS, 46). It focuses primarily on marriage and the family, in the conviction that “the well-being of the individual and of human and Christian society is intimately linked with the healthy condition of that community produced by marriage and family” (GS, 47). To this end, it does not merely reaffirm their values and aims, but proposes a renewed conception of marriage as an “intimate partnership of married life and love” (GS, 48). By incorporating the legal dimension of marriage as a contract, the foundation of this union is recognized in the “conjugal covenant”, understood as the “human act whereby spouses mutually bestow and accept each another” (ibid.). The mutual self-giving of man and woman, such that ‘they are no longer two but one flesh’ (Mt 19:6), underlies the requirement for “total fidelity” and the “unbreakable oneness” of the spouses, finding vivid expression in the procreation and upbringing of children (cf. GS, 48). As a reflection of the Divine Trinity, conjugal and parental love, through the Sacrament of Marriage, is “governed and enriched by Christ’s redeeming power”, so that spouses may love one another “just as He loved the Church and handed Himself over on her behalf” (ibid.). Having shed light on the reality of marriage in the light of Christ’s love, which is the truth of both human and divine love, Gaudium et Spes turns its attention to conjugal love and marital fruitfulness. Not limited to erotic attraction, which it nonetheless encompasses, conjugal love involves the entire will of the spouses, enlivening the affections of their hearts and expressing itself through sentiments and gestures of tenderness (cf. GS, 49). Embracing the good of the whole person of both man and woman, who are equal in dignity, this love pervades the entire life of the spouses, finding expression in acts proper exclusively to marriage (cf. ibid.). Whilst signifying integral love from person to person, the unique intimacy between the spouses fosters their mutual self-giving and enriches their shared joy (cf. ibid.). Furthermore, the fruitfulness of conjugal love is expressed in the procreation of children, “the supreme gift of marriage” (GS, 50). By transmitting and educating human life, which must never be rejected, spouses become “cooperators with the love of God the Creator, and are, so to speak, the interpreters of that love” (ibid.). Called to this human and Christian responsibility, they are bound to allow themselves to be guided by a sound judgement regarding their own good and that of their children, whether already born or yet to be born. Such a judgement, which, in the final analysis, the spouses themselves must form before God, requires that their conscience conform to divine law, as interpreted by the Magisterium of the Church in the light of the Gospel (cf. ibid.). The emphasis on loving communion and procreative fruitfulness within marriage leads the Council to rule out the possibility of there being “a true contradiction … between the divine laws pertaining to the transmission of life, and those pertaining to authentic conjugal love” (GS, 51) and to affirm, instead, that “when there is question of harmonizing conjugal love with the responsible transmission of life”, one must “preserve the full sense of mutual self-giving and human procreation in the context of true love” (ibid.). From this it follows both that “from the moment of its conception life must be guarded with the greatest care”, renouncing “abortion and infanticide”; and that “the acts themselves which are proper to conjugal love and which are exercised in accord with genuine human dignity must be honoured with great reverence” (ibid.). The teaching of Gaudium et Spes on the conjugal and family community thus goes on to highlight the social function of the family, defined as “a school of deeper humanity” and “the foundation of society” (GS, 52), calling upon all those with social responsibilities, especially in the political and cultural spheres, to fulfil their duty to “work efficiently for the welfare of marriage and the family” (ibid.). Dear friends, this task is more urgent than ever before. The Church is well aware of this, as shown by the pastoral concern of the Popes who have succeeded one another since the last Council, right up to the two Synodal Assemblies convened by Pope Francis, which were addressed again in recent days by the Heads of the Eastern Catholic Churches and the Presidents of the Episcopal Conferences. A year ago this week, Julia Scheib (AUT/Rossignol) entered the season opener in Sölden as a 27-year-old with no career World Cup victories, just one individual podium, and a best title-race finish of ninth in her preferred Giant Slalom discipline. The Austrian unexpectedly grabbed her her first World Cup win on home snow on the Rettenbach glacier that October weekend, and she added four more triumphs over the winter to power a surprisingly dominant Crystal Globe-winning campaign. As Scheib and the rest of the world's best technical skiers again gather in Sölden to kick-start another year of high adrenaline and emotions on the Giant Slalom slopes, the question on everyone's lips is: Who will be this season's Julia Scheib? In a way, Zrinka Ljutic's (CRO/Atomic) 2025/26 season was the opposite of Scheib's. The young Croatian entered the campaign as one of the hottest emerging names in the sport, but endured a difficult winter. Following her breakout 2024/25 season, in which she won three races and the Slalom globe, Ljutic managed only one podium last year, in Giant Slalom in Tremblant. Now, at age 22, she is ready to resume her place among the elite. "Last season taught me a lot about patience, resilience, and trusting my own process, especially when things don’t go as planned," Ljutic said this week. "I’ve learned that progress isn’t always linear, and that the most important thing is how you respond to the difficult moments. "I want to take that experience into this winter with a clearer mindset, stay focused on my skiing, and continue building with confidence." To get back to the top, Ljutic made some changes over the summer, working with a new strength and conditioning coach, and training in New Zealand for the first time for a five-week period during the Southern Hemisphere winter. Additionally, her father, Amir, will serve as both her coach and ski technician this season, which Zrinka sees as a crucial dual role within her team. "We know each other very well, and I believe that having him involved in both aspects will be valuable as we continue to work towards our goals," she said. This Saturday, Ljutic will face the first test in seeing whether her new approach and hard work has paid off. "There’s something unique about opening the season on the Rettenbach glacier, with its demanding terrain, the incredible atmosphere, and the passion of the Austrian fans," she said. "The hill requires both precision and commitment, especially on the steep section, where finding the right rhythm is essential." If Ljutic can locate that rhythm, both in Sölden and throughout the season, she will once again be a name to look out for. The 27-year-old emerged as the biggest duel technical threat on the tour last year, finishing second in both the Giant Slalom and Slalom globe races, in addition to third in the Overall standings. This season, she will take aim at all those titles, as well as going for gold at the world championships in February in her home town of Crans-Montana. "Last season was a great one, and I want to keep building on that," Rast said this week. "Competing in both Slalom and GS is important to me, so my focus is on finding consistency and improving in both disciplines." Although she can glimpse those potential Crystal Globes and world championship medals sparkling on the horizon, Rast is not getting ahead of herself. "I think it will be an interesting and competitive season," she said. "There are many strong athletes, and I prefer to focus on my own skiing rather than on who is racing or not. "Of course, racing World Championships at home will be very special. But it’s still a long season, with many important races in both disciplines. I’ll take it step by step and focus on each race as it comes." That starts on Saturday in Sölden, which hasn't been a happy hunting ground for Rast in the past. Her best result in the season opener was 12th in 2024, while last year she came 15th, her only finish outside the top six in Giant Slalom during the entire World Cup season other than one DNF. "We’ve been working on different things over the summer, including some issues related to last year’s injury," Rast said of her preparation for the season ahead. "It’s still a work in progress, but overall the preparation has been positive. Sölden will be a good opportunity to see where I stand." Where she stands? On the podium on Saturday, if everything goes to plan. It's hard to believe Alice Robinson (NZL/Head) is still only 24 years old, since it seems like a bygone era when she burst onto the scene in Sölden at just 17 in pre-Covid times. "Sölden is a really special place for me," Robinson said this week. "I had my first World Cup win here seven years ago, which is pretty crazy to think about." Since that breakout win in 2019, Robinson has gone through her fair share of ups and downs. Last season, she was in a fierce battle with Scheib for the Giant Slalom lead with two early race wins, only to fall away in the second part of the season. "Last season was probably my most successful on paper, with some incredible moments and strong performances, but also some tough setbacks," said Robinson, who also won her first World Cup Super G race last December. "I learned the importance of staying present, focusing on the task at hand and controlling the small details rather than getting caught up in the bigger picture." With three straight top-five finishes in the GS season standings under her belt, and a change of equipment this year, Robinson is primed for her best season yet — if she can bring her A-game every week. "I know that to be right up there, I need to be executing every run, and that’s the goal," she said. "It’s about being consistent across different slopes and conditions, and really bringing my GS back to its best. "I know I have the speed, so it’s about putting all the pieces together throughout the season and giving myself the best opportunity to fight for the globe." That all begins in Sölden, a hill the young veteran knows well, having registered two podiums and four other top-12 finishes already at the Austrian resort. "There’s something special about the atmosphere, the energy and the anticipation around the season kicking off," she said. "There’s always so much excitement, and it’s a really cool time to be part of the sport. "The hill itself is also a great challenge. That long, sustained pitch is probably one of the toughest on the women’s circuit. "I think the race is a lot about having the confidence to commit, especially in the first race of the season. It rewards technically sound skiing and good tactics, which is what makes it so fun to ski and to watch." The most successful World Cup ski racer of all-time, Mikaela Shiffrin (USA/Atomic), hopes a new approach this season will complete her long journey back to the top of a Giant Slalom podium. Remarkably, Shiffrin sometimes flies under the radar as a Giant Slalom skier, given her incredible Slalom dominance that has yielded an unfathomable 73 World Cup wins on the short skis alone. Yet her 22 World Cup wins in Giant Slalom is also more than any other women's racer, plus she won the Olympic GS title in 2018. However, it's been far from smooth sailing in recent years for Shiffrin in Giant Slalom. Following the puncture wound she suffered in a GS race in Killington in November 2024, she spoke openly about her resulting PTSD and difficulty in coming back to the discipline. She hasn't won a World Cup Giant Slalom race since December 2023, but fought hard last season for one podium and seven other top-six finishes. "Last season was crazy because I started the season thinking I might get kicked out of the top 30 and that might be sort of the beginning of the end of GS for me," the American said on her podcast, What's the Point with Mikaela Shiffrin, this month. "And then having the goal of actually working back into the top seven (the top-seeded group of athletes for start order), having that actually happen and seeing that I have speed in GS even where fear exists." This season, Shiffrin will limit her Slalom races to focus almost exclusively on Giant Slalom and Super G, tackling her fear head-on. "I can have a relationship with that fear," the 110-time World Cup winner said on her podcast. "It's just the last two years, I've learned so, so much about mentality and psychology and fear. "And I'm sure that's going to be an ongoing thing, but it gives me so much excitement to explore what that means with GS and with Super G." Far from being almost washed up in Giant Slalom as she once thought, the 31-year-old is now left with a feeling that, with Sölden just days away, might instill some fear into some of her rivals, too. "I really wonder where I can take GS skiing," Shiffrin said. Possibly still underrated despite her stellar 2026 campaign, Scheib can become the first woman to win back-to-back Giant Slalom Crystal Globes since compatriot Anna Veith (née Fenninger, AUT) in 2014 and 2015. This year, however, the defending World Cup champion will have a target on her back from the moment she puts on the red bib on Saturday. Beyond Ljutic, Rast, Robinson and Shiffrin, a combination of veterans and young stars will all fancy their chances for a shot at the Giant Slalom Crystal Globe. Among them, experienced Swede Sara Hector (SWE/Head), the 2022 Olympic Giant Slalom champion, has finished third in the GS season standings in each of the last three seasons and has shown no signs of slowing down at age 34. She finished in the top four in seven of the 10 World Cup giant slalom races last year and also grabbed a joint silver at Milano Cortina 2026 with Thea Louise Stjernesund (NOR/Rossignol), who also figures to contend again this year. The winner of that Olympic race, the brilliant Federica Brignone (ITA/Rossignol), will miss Sölden while rehabilitating from surgery she underwent in August after her remarkable double gold performance on home snow in February. However, the reigning Olympic and world Giant Slalom champion will undoubtedly be a factor in the globe race once the winter gets going, even at 36 years old. A skier just over half Brignone's age, 19-year-old Lara Colturi (ALB/Head), is perhaps the most promising talent of the next generation. With seven World Cup podiums already in the technical disciplines, her first victory can't be far away. Colturi came seventh in Sölden last year and has improved every time she has returned to the Rettenbach glacier in her young career, making her a name to watch on Saturday and throughout the year. All in all, the women's Giant Slalom field could hardly be better placed to deliver a fabulous season opener as the launching pad into an unpredictable globe chase. "GS is extremely competitive at the moment, with a great mix of experienced veterans and young guns coming through," Robinson said. The 2027 Audi FIS World Cup season begins on Saturday with the women's Giant Slalom race in Sölden, Austria, at 10:00/13:00 CET.

title: Colombian Star Karol G’s ‘BbY WOW’ Outlasts Taylor Swift for Sixth Week Atop Global 200 - Martin Cid Magazine
content: Karol G’s “BbY WOW” is back on top of Billboard’s global charts, and the most telling part of its run is what it had to beat to stay there. For one week, Taylor Swift’s “Patient Zero” took the crown with exactly the kind of launch the modern music business is built to produce. The following week, the song Karol G made with Spanish artists Judeline and rusowsky took it back, and it has held on since. That is an odd career for a track nobody planned as the biggest hit of her life. “BbY WOW” started as a Karol G solo song and became a trio late, when she reopened it to two artists from Spain’s alternative scene. Its climb was already underway before the dance trend that much of the coverage credits for its rise. Up close, the streaming giant of the autumn looks less like a campaign and more like a last-minute creative call that paid off. Billboard’s own numbers make the contrast plain. “Patient Zero,” one of four new songs on Swift’s deluxe edition The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, opened at No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200 and Global Excl. U.S. charts dated Oct. 10 with 70.7 million streams and 80,000 copies sold worldwide, according to Luminate. “BbY WOW” slipped to No. 3 that week after four weeks on top. Seven days later it was No. 1 again with 46.2 million streams while “Patient Zero” fell to No. 2, and on the charts dated Oct. 24 Swift’s single sits at No. 3. The new tracking week, Oct. 9 to 15, gave “BbY WOW” 45.4 million streams worldwide, down just 2% from the week before, plus 1,000 copies sold. About three of every four of those streams, 34.1 million, came from outside the United States. Shakira and Burna Boy’s World Cup anthem “Dai Dai” owned the summer before “BbY WOW” ended its reign in September; Billboard noted at the time that Karol G’s song was the first No. 1 on the global charts performed mostly in Spanish since Bad Bunny’s “DtMF” finished its run in March. For Karol G, it is new territory. Her only previous leader on the lists, “TQG” with Shakira, topped them for its debut week in March 2023. “BbY WOW” gave her a first multi-week global No. 1 in September and, in the U.S., her second Hot 100 top 10 after that same Shakira duet. How the song reached its final shape is the part the chart celebrations skip. Judeline told NYLON that she wrote with Karol G in Malibu, with Tainy and rusowsky in the room, while the Colombian star was rehearsing for Coachella, and that “BbY WOW” “was supposed to be a song for her and only her.” About two weeks before the album came out, Karol called asking for Judeline and rusowsky on it. “We did the song in two days,” Judeline said. She cut her verse in a studio she tracked down near her hometown, hidden behind what looked from the street like a fried-fish shop, and the song was out a week later. Karol G described the same decision to Rolling Stone, as quoted by Songfacts: “The first version was just me. But I felt like, live, I wanted to sing that song with more people on stage and for it to turn into a party.” The credits carry that collaborative streak. Karol, Tainy, Omer Fedi, Judeline and rusowsky all share production, over a flip of the Coolie Dance Riddim that Nina Sky’s “Move Ya Body” made famous in 2004. Judeline’s hand on the album goes well beyond the feature: she co-wrote four songs on No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, including the opener “Te Llevas To.” In France, NRJ framed the run as the work of a TikTok choreography by the creator trio Los Menor3s, posted on Aug. 24, whom Karol later brought on stage during her U.S. tour. The trend was real and it spread fast. The chart timeline, though, says it poured fuel on a fire that was already lit. The song entered Spotify’s global daily chart on Aug. 12, according to La República, and jumped from No. 171 to No. 37 on the Global 200 in the tracking week that closed on Aug. 20, Complex reported, four days before the dance went up. The weeks that followed, a 37-to-5 leap on a 45% gain in streams and then the move to No. 1, are where the song and the trend pushed together. There is a fair caveat inside all of this. Billboard’s global charts blend official streams and download sales from more than 200 territories, and in practice they are streaming rankings: “BbY WOW” sells around 1,000 copies a week worldwide. “Biggest song in the world” now means the song most replayed on platforms where playlists and short-video trends do much of the distribution. That system rewards a huge opening, as Swift’s week showed. It also rewards the songs listeners keep returning to, which is how a track that sold a fraction of her copies took the top spot back. For the two Spaniards, the scale has changed completely. Judeline, who grew up in Cádiz, became the first Spanish woman to reach No. 1 on Spotify’s global chart, according to LatiNation and N+. In 2024 she played London’s The Lower Third to 250 people; on Sept. 5 she closed her first headlining tour in front of 26,500 at Plaza Mayor in Valladolid, she told NYLON. rusowsky, the Madrid producer and singer born Ruslán Mediavilla and known for his bedroom-pop records, scored his first Hot 100 top 10 alongside her. No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, Karol G’s sixth studio album, came out Aug. 7 and debuted at No. 1 on Top Latin Albums. Her tour is still working through the Americas and reaches Europe next year, opening in Barcelona on June 3, 2027, with Paris on July 1. The song Karol G first recorded alone has already spent six times as many weeks at No. 1 on Billboard’s global chart as the rest of her catalog combined.
